All stages are planned; none is declared closed or implemented.

nodes.title: Berkovich spectrum
nodes.statement: For a normed commutative unital ring A, M(A) is the subtype of native MulRingSeminorm A consisting of p with p(a) ≤ ‖a‖ for every a. Points are actual real-valued seminorms, not equivalence classes. Completeness, a base field, multiplicativity of the ambient norm and a nonarchimedean norm are not required for this carrier.
proofSteps: Take the norm-dominated subtype of the existing seminorm carrier; retain its function coercion through the named evaluation projection. The native carrier already supplies positivity, zero, negation, triangle inequality, one and multiplication.
acceptance: The zero ring has no point because one must map to one and zero to zero.
The zero function is excluded.
On the product of two real fields, the two projection seminorms are distinct; the ambient maximum norm itself is not multiplicative.

sources.match: The source uses bounded points for Banach rings. The bounded-iff-dominated node proves equality with this presentation; this carrier needs no completion.

nodes.title: Bounded points are norm dominated
nodes.statement: For p in native MulRingSeminorm A, there is a constant C>0 with p(a)≤C‖a‖ for all a if and only if p(a)≤‖a‖ for all a.
proofSteps: Apply the native contraction theorem to the identity ring map, the norm ring seminorm, and the multiplicative function p. Native preservation of powers supplies power multiplicativity.
For the reverse direction choose C=1. This is an adapter, not a second power-trick theorem.
acceptance: A different positive bound C produces the same point subtype.
A point need not be bounded as a real-valued function on all of A.

proofSteps: Use the native induced topology on the native function product.
Apply the inducing-map continuity criterion, followed by coordinatewise continuity into a product.

The two projection points of ℝ×ℝ have disjoint separating neighborhoods.

nodes.statement: The evaluation map M(A)→ℝ^A is a topological embedding.
proofSteps: The topology is induced by definition. Native seminorm extensionality and subtype extensionality prove injectivity.

nodes.title: Equations for the evaluation image
nodes.statement: The image of M(A) in ℝ^A is exactly the functions v satisfying v(0)=0, v(1)=1, v(−a)=v(a), v(a+b)≤v(a)+v(b), v(ab)=v(a)v(b), and 0≤v(a)≤‖a‖ for all a,b.
proofSteps: Unpack a spectrum point to obtain the listed laws.
Conversely bundle the additive group seminorm laws and multiplicative zero-preserving unital homomorphism laws into the existing MulRingSeminorm, then attach domination.
acceptance: The zero function violates the one equation; the product maximum norm violates multiplication.

sources.match: Native-carrier expansion used only to prove the image description.

nodes.title: Closedness of the evaluation image
nodes.statement: The image of M(A) in ℝ^A is closed.
proofSteps: Express the image as the intersection of the equalities and inequalities of evaluation-range.

Coordinate evaluation, real addition and real multiplication are continuous. Each equality is closed by the Hausdorff equality theorem; each inequality is closed by the real order theorem. Intersect over all elements and pairs.
acceptance: One uses non-strict inequalities; imposing strict positivity on all nonzero elements would fail closedness.

sources.match: This is the explicit topological proof step for the compactness statement; supplied here from native closed-set lemmas.

nodes.title: Compactness of the Berkovich spectrum
nodes.statement: M(A) is compact for every normed commutative ring A, even without completeness or nontriviality.
proofSteps: The image lies in the product of compact real intervals [0,‖a‖]. Tychonoff makes that product compact.
Closedness of the image makes it a compact subset of this product. Reflect compactness along the evaluation embedding. No nonemptiness argument is used.
acceptance: M(ℝ×ℝ) is compact although its ambient norm is not multiplicative.
The empty spectrum of a zero ring is compact.

sources.match: Proves the compactness assertion in a stronger generality; the nonemptiness assertion is not included.

nodes.title: Hausdorffness of the Berkovich spectrum

acceptance: Projection points on ℝ×ℝ are separated using evaluation at (2,3).

sources.match: Point separation follows from distinct real-valued seminorms having different coordinates.

nodes.title: Pullback of Berkovich points
nodes.statement: For normed commutative rings A,B and a bounded unital ring homomorphism f:A→B, construct the continuous map M(f):M(B)→M(A), given by M(f)(x)(a)=x(f(a)).
proofSteps: Compose the native seminorm laws with the ring map. If ‖f(a)‖≤C‖a‖, then x(f(a))≤C‖a‖. Apply bounded-iff-dominated to the composed seminorm.
For continuity test each a-coordinate, which is evaluation at f(a). Identity and reversed composition follow by pointwise extensionality.
acceptance: Contravariance reverses f:A→B and g:B→D: M(g∘f)=M(f)∘M(g).
Do not assume an arbitrary continuous ring homomorphism is bounded.

sources.match: Contravariant continuous functor on bounded homomorphisms; completeness is unused.

nodes.title: Seminormed Banach rings
nodes.statement: Use commutative unital seminormed rings with submultiplicative seminorm and |1|≤1, including the zero ring, then separated completion. Morphisms in the colimit statements are contractive unital maps. M(A) consists of unital multiplicative real seminorms dominated by the specified seminorm. The normed-ring subtype already planned embeds this general carrier after separation.
hypotheses: A seminorm, rather than merely its topology, is part of the data.
proofSteps: Quotient the seminorm-zero ideal, complete the resulting metric ring, and extend multiplication by uniform continuity on bounded sets. Every dominated multiplicative seminorm kills that ideal and extends uniquely through completion.
acceptance: Use commutative unital seminormed rings with submultiplicative seminorm and |1|≤1, including the zero ring, then separated completion. Morphisms in the colimit statements are contractive unital maps. M(A) consists of unital multiplicative real seminorms dominated by the specified seminorm. nodes.title: Existence of spectral points
nodes.statement: A nonzero complete commutative unital seminormed Banach ring with |1|=1 has nonempty spectrum; its spectrum is compact Hausdorff. A completion that becomes zero is excluded.
hypotheses: Nonzero separated complete Banach ring; norm of one is one.
proofSteps: For existence use Berkovich’s maximal-ideal quotient and minimal bounded-seminorm construction; the weighted power-series contradiction forces multiplicativity. Compactness and Hausdorffness use the inherited closed evaluation-image proof, which does not require completeness.
acceptance: The zero-ring exception is necessary.
The archimedean and trivial absolute-value field cases are included.

sources.match: Supplies existence, including the part not implied by compactness.
Records the general Banach-ring version and unit normalization.

nodes.title: Units and spectral maximum
nodes.statement: For a complete nonzero commutative Banach ring A, a is a unit iff x(a)>0 for every x∈M(A). Moreover ρ(a)=limₙ||aⁿ||^(1/n)=infₙ≥1||aⁿ||^(1/n)=maxₓ x(a). The spectrum is unchanged by replacing the seminorm with its spectral uniformization and taking separated completion.
hypotheses: Unital Banach norm normalized at one; positive integer powers in the infimum.
proofSteps: Apply nonemptiness to the quotient by a maximal ideal containing a for the unit test. Test invertibility of 1−aT in weighted convergent series rings to obtain the sharp spectral-radius bound, then use compactness for attainment. The power trick gives the reverse inequality.
acceptance: A nonzero nilpotent has spectral radius zero.
In ℝ×ℝ the radius is max(|a|,|b|), not a multiplicative norm.

sources.match: Gives unit detection and the spectral maximum, rather than only a definition by infimum.
Relates spectral uniformization to the same spectrum.

nodes.title: Completed residue fields
nodes.statement: For x∈M(A), ker(x) is prime, x descends to an absolute value on Frac(A/ker(x)), and H(x) is its completion. Evaluation A→H(x) has absolute value x. Bounded pullback f*:M(B)→M(A) induces an isometric field embedding H(f*x)→H(x).
hypotheses: A commutative normed ring; x a normalized dominated multiplicative seminorm.
proofSteps: Multiplicativity makes the kernel prime; define |a/b|=x(a)/x(b), prove independence and complete. Extend the induced fraction-field embedding uniquely to completions.
acceptance: For x∈M(A), ker(x) is prime, x descends to an absolute value on Frac(A/ker(x)), and H(x) is its completion. Evaluation A→H(x) has absolute value x. Bounded pullback f*:M(B)→M(A) induces an isometric field embedding H(f*x)→H(x).

nodes.title: Valued base change of spectra
nodes.statement: For complete nonarchimedean K, a K-affinoid algebra A and complete valued extension L/K, M(A⊗̂_K L)→M(A) is continuous proper surjective. For a finite normal extension it is the topological quotient by the separable Galois group, with purely inseparable extension inducing a homeomorphism. Completed algebraic closure has the corresponding Galois quotient.

proofSteps: A point lifts by amalgamating H(x) and L over K and evaluating in a common complete valued field. Compactness gives properness in the affinoid case. Normal-extension orbit classification is checked on residue fields, then passed to the completed algebraic closure.

nodes.title: Spectra and contractive colimits
nodes.statement: In the category of commutative Banach rings and contractive maps, complete separated projective ℓ¹ tensor products compute pushouts. The induced map M(B⊗̂_A C)→M(B)×_{M(A)}M(C) is surjective. Filtered colimits, formed by seminormed colimit and separated completion, have spectrum canonically homeomorphic to the inverse limit of the spectra. All small colimits exist in this category; ℤ with its usual absolute value is initial.
hypotheses: The tensor norm is the projective ℓ¹ norm in the general archimedean category. Nonarchimedean affinoid tensor norms are a separate specialization.
proofSteps: For compatible points use valued-field amalgamation to obtain a bounded tensor evaluation. For filtered colimits compatible seminorms define a single dominated seminorm on the algebraic colimit, then extend to completion; compact Hausdorff topology identifies the inverse limit.
acceptance: For ℂ⊗̂_ℝℂ, the two conjugate factors give two points over the single pair of field-norm points: injectivity fails.
Do not replace ℓ¹ by a maximum tensor seminorm in the archimedean category.
Every unital ring map ℤ→A is contractive because ||n·1||≤|n|. A trivially normed ℤ would not be initial in the archimedean category.

sources.match: Pushout comparison is surjective, not an asserted homeomorphism; filtered-colimit comparison is a homeomorphism.
Computes the contractive category colimits using infimum quotient/projective ℓ¹ seminorms and separated completion.

nodes.title: Affinoid algebras over valued fields

Strict affinoids admit a presentation with radii 1. Morphisms are bounded K-algebra maps and presentations are auxiliary data.
hypotheses: K may be trivially valued; radii need not belong to |K×|.
proofSteps: Use convergent power series with coefficientwise ring operations; prove the Gauss norm multiplicative, completeness and universal evaluation on bounded tuples. Separate quotient norms and prove equivalent presentations define the same bounded algebra.
acceptance: For complete nonarchimedean K and positive radii r, K{r⁻¹T} consists of series with |a_I|r^I→0, with weighted Gauss norm; a K-affinoid algebra is a Banach quotient of one. Strict affinoids admit a presentation with radii 1. Morphisms are bounded K-algebra maps and presentations are auxiliary data.

nodes.title: Analytic atlases and morphisms

nodes.title: Normalized rank-one adic quotient
nodes.statement: Let A be a nonarchimedean Banach ring with a uniform topologically nilpotent unit z, A⁺ an open integrally closed subring of the power-bounded ring A°, and Spa(A,A⁺) the native adic spectrum. Normalization of rank-one valuations gives a section M(A)→Spa(A,A⁺); every adic point has a unique maximal rank-one generization and the resulting map r:Spa(A,A⁺)→M(A) is a continuous retraction and the maximal Hausdorff quotient. The section is not asserted continuous.
hypotheses: Uniform unit, not merely arbitrary nonzero topologically nilpotent element. Use equivalence classes of valuations on Spa, normalized real seminorms on M(A).
The plus ring is allowed to be smaller than A°; a complete Tate Huber pair with such a norm is included. The quotient is independent of A⁺, while Spa need not be.

For a general complete Tate Huber pair, choose the z-adic Banach gauge from the uniform-unit hierarchy first. This is an existence statement for a suitable norm, not a retraction onto the spectrum for every compatible Banach norm.
proofSteps: Normalize via z and the infimum over comparisons of powers described in KL 2.4.6. Show the maximal generization is independent of z; rational encircling neighborhoods prove continuity and the Hausdorff universal property.
acceptance: Do not identify the whole Spa point set with M(A).
Changing A⁺ can change the adic point set; for the fixed uniform-unit norm its maximal Hausdorff quotient is M(A).
A claim with a merely topologically nilpotent element must not replace the uniform-unit hypothesis.

sources.locator: Definition 2.4.1 and Remark 2.4.4, pp. 37–39; Definitions 2.4.6, 2.4.8, p. 40
sources.match: The normalization and maximal Hausdorff quotient work for the full adic Banach pair (A,A⁺), not only A⁺=A°. A uniform unit is the stated norm hypothesis.

nodes.title: Strict Berkovich–adic equivalence
nodes.statement: Over a complete nontrivially valued rank-one field K, Hausdorff strictly K-analytic Berkovich spaces are equivalent to taut adic spaces locally of finite type over Spa(K,K°). On an affinoid Spa(A,A°), its maximal-point quotient is M(A), and adic affinoid opens correspond to Berkovich affinoid domains. Partially proper maps give boundaryless maps; proper maps give proper maps; étale maps give quasi-étale maps; smooth maps give quasi-smooth maps. For partially proper maps, adic étaleness is equivalent to Berkovich étaleness; partially proper smooth maps are Berkovich smooth. Quasi-étaleness alone is not declared étaleness.
hypotheses: Hausdorff strict and taut locally finite-type hypotheses; arbitrary locally noetherian adic spaces and nonstrict Berkovich spaces are outside this equivalence.
proofSteps: Glue the normalized affinoid comparison along domain intersections. Tautness gives the correct separated quotient topology. For morphisms use the reduction/germ criterion for absence of relative boundary, then the stated local étale and smooth comparisons. The categorical equivalence proof invokes the precise Huber comparison input in the gaps.
acceptance: Over a complete nontrivially valued rank-one field K, Hausdorff strictly K-analytic Berkovich spaces are equivalent to taut adic spaces locally of finite type over Spa(K,K°). On an affinoid Spa(A,A°), its maximal-point quotient is M(A), and adic affinoid opens correspond to Berkovich affinoid domains. Partially proper maps give boundaryless maps; proper maps give proper maps; étale maps give quasi-étale maps; smooth maps give quasi-smooth maps.

nodes.title: Real quotient of analytic preadic spaces
nodes.statement: For a preadic space over an analytic field, identify points with the same maximal normalized rank-one generization and equip the set of these generizations with the quotient topology. Partially proper opens are the saturated inverse images of opens in this real quotient. For an adic space, quasi-compactness descends to the real quotient without a tautness hypothesis; if the space is taut its real quotient is Hausdorff and is its maximal Hausdorff quotient, and every partially proper open is taut.
hypotheses: The tautness condition is essential for the global maximal Hausdorff assertion; use the KL analytic-field normalization.
proofSteps: Glue the local rank-one quotient sets and topologies. A continuous quotient preserves quasi-compactness. Tautness gives separation of distinct rank-one points; any continuous map to a Hausdorff space is constant on generization classes. For a partially proper open, the image of a quasi-compact open has compact, hence closed, image in the Hausdorff quotient; its saturated inverse image contains its closure and stays inside the partially proper open. Together with quasiseparatedness this proves tautness.
acceptance: The doubled-origin closed disc has a non-Hausdorff real quotient, so the tautness qualification cannot be removed.
A partially proper open in a taut adic space remains taut even if it is not quasi-compact.

nodes.title: Hybrid analytic spaces
nodes.statement: For a projective meromorphic family X over a punctured complex disc, choose 0<r<1 small enough for its defining coefficients. The Banach ring A_r of convergent Laurent series uses coefficient hybrid norm max(|c|∞,|c|triv) and weight rⁿ. Its spectrum is the closed disc; the associated analytic family has usual complex fibers for t≠0 and central fiber at parameter 0 equal to X_{ℂ((t))}ᵃⁿ, where the formal parameter has nonarchimedean absolute value r. The topology makes |f|^{log r/log|t|} converge to its nonarchimedean evaluation; the SNC-model hybrid inverse limit gives the same space.
hypotheses: Projective meromorphic family; the Laurent series have finitely many negative terms and finite weighted hybrid sum; fix r within the convergence radius.

The complex family is a smooth projective submersion meromorphic at 0; shrink to the closed disc of radius r. The analytic-space machinery must include general Banach-ring bases, not just nonarchimedean K-affinoid charts.
proofSteps: Build the hybrid Banach base, identify nonzero fibers with powered complex absolute values and the zero fiber with the t-adic completion. Compare affinoid evaluations with SNC-model logarithmic coordinates and pass to the model inverse limit.

nodes.title: Uniform Gelfand representation
nodes.statement: For a uniform commutative Banach ring A, the evaluation homomorphism A→∏_{x∈M(A)}H(x) is isometric for the supremum norm: ||a||=max_x|a(x)|. For arbitrary A its kernel is the spectral seminorm-zero ideal, not necessarily zero.
hypotheses: Uniform means the given complete norm is power-multiplicative.
proofSteps: For a nonzero element in a power-multiplicative ring, adjoin its inverse with inverse norm bounded by its reciprocal. Power multiplicativity keeps the norm of one equal to one. Nonemptiness of this Banach localization produces a field-valued evaluation attaining the original norm. The spectral maximum then identifies the Gelfand kernel and the isometric uniform representation.
acceptance: The dual numbers have a nonzero element in the kernel before uniformization.

sources.match: The uniform Gelfand transform is an isometric embedding.
The spectral/Gelfand kernel is the seminorm-zero ideal.

nodes.title: Idempotents and clopen subsets

hypotheses: Complete commutative Banach ring with normalized unit.
proofSteps: Multiplicativity restricts x(e) to 0 or 1 and the unit test gives uniqueness. Lift idempotents by Newton iteration from the uniform completion. For a two-domain spectral cover, the overconvergent Laurent equalizer glues compatible idempotents. Refine a clopen partition by finitely many such domains; complementing the vanishing-locus convention gives the stated value-one convention. The closed-ideal/equalizer input in KL Corollary 2.8.9 remains to be checked in full.

nodes.title: Connected algebraic curves remain connected

nodes.title: Uniform units and trivial spectrum
nodes.statement: A topologically nilpotent element satisfies ||aⁿ||→0. A uniform unit is an invertible topologically nilpotent z with ρ(z)ρ(z⁻¹)=1. A Banach ring is free of trivial spectrum when every H(x) has nontrivial absolute value; equivalently the ideal generated by its topologically nilpotent elements is the unit ideal. For nonzero nonarchimedean Banach rings, being a bounded Banach algebra over an analytic field implies admitting a uniform unit, which implies admitting a topologically nilpotent unit, which implies freedom of trivial spectrum. The converse from a uniform unit to an analytic-field algebra in characteristic p requires additional norm control, for example equivalence of the norm with the spectral norm.
hypotheses: The Banach ring is nonzero and separated complete. An analytic field is complete and nontrivially valued. All scalar homomorphisms in the hierarchy are bounded for the specified norms.
proofSteps: The spectral maximum and the inverse identity force x(z)=ρ(z) for every spectral point. Apply the unit criterion to the ideal of topologically nilpotent elements for the trivial-spectrum characterization. A topologically nilpotent scalar from the analytic base field gives a uniform unit. In characteristic p and a uniform Banach ring, the estimates on all positive and negative powers of z extend the Laurent-series map from F_p((z)) boundedly. For a complete Tate Huber ring choose a ring of definition A₀ containing the pseudouniformizer and use the z-adic gauge norm; this selects a uniform normalization rather than proving the original norm already had it.
acceptance: A topologically nilpotent element satisfies ||aⁿ||→0. A uniform unit is an invertible topologically nilpotent z with ρ(z)ρ(z⁻¹)=1. A Banach ring is free of trivial spectrum when every H(x) has nontrivial absolute value; equivalently the ideal generated by its topologically nilpotent elements is the unit ideal. For nonzero nonarchimedean Banach rings, being a bounded Banach algebra over an analytic field implies admitting a uniform unit, which implies admitting a topologically nilpotent unit, which implies freedom of trivial spectrum. The converse from a uniform unit to an analytic-field algebra in characteristic p requires additional norm control, for example equivalence of the norm with the spectral norm.

nodes.title: Surjectivity detected by residue fields
nodes.statement: For an A-linear map M→N over a nonarchimedean Banach ring A, with N finitely generated, surjectivity is equivalent to surjectivity of M⊗_A H(x)→N⊗_A H(x) for every x∈M(A). If B is faithfully finite étale over A with its finite Banach module topology, M(B)→M(A) is surjective; under the uniform-unit hypotheses of Hausdorff localization it is also open.
hypotheses: No topology or finite-generation hypothesis is imposed on M. The displayed module tensors are algebraic. N must be finite. Étale openness uses the same analytic hypotheses as KL §2.4.
proofSteps: The cokernel is finite. For each maximal ideal choose a spectral point with that kernel by the closed maximal-ideal quotient construction. Faithful scalar extension from its residue field to H(x), followed by Nakayama, annihilates the localized cokernel; hence it vanishes. For finite étale B, the completed fiber over H(x) is a nonzero product of finite valued-field extensions. Its nonempty spectrum lifts x. The Hausdorff-localization factorization proves openness.
acceptance: The zero map to A is detected at every spectral residue field when A is nonzero.
Faithfulness excludes a finite étale algebra supported on only one factor of a product ring.
Openness and surjectivity are distinct assertions; the finite étale hypothesis alone does not remove the faithfulness requirement for surjectivity.

nodes.title: Four types of points

nodes.title: Paths, tangent directions and hyperbolic metric

nodes.statement: Let f∈K(X)× on smooth proper X, and choose a marked skeleton containing all zeros and poles as punctures. F=−log|f| is integral-affine along the extended edges, constant on complementary balls and harmonic at every unmarked nonclassical point. At type II, its outgoing slope equals the order of the normalized residue function in that branch; along a ray toward P the outgoing slope is ord_P(f). On a compact skeleton Δ(F|Γ)=τ_*div(f), equivalently divPL(log|f||Γ)=τ_*div(f).
hypotheses: K algebraically closed complete nontrivial; include the support of div(f) in the marking.
proofSteps: Use analytic-unit constancy on balls and Laurent slopes on annuli. In a formal node chart compare the first nonvanishing residue term with its annular exponent. The principal divisor on the residue curve has degree zero, proving harmonicity; cancel attached branch fluxes to obtain the compact-graph formula.
acceptance: On G_m, F=−log|T| has slope +1 toward 0 and −1 toward infinity.
The compact formula uses Δ rather than divPL for −log|f|.

nodes.title: Metrized complexes and their divisors
nodes.statement: A metrized complex consists of compact Γ, a smooth proper connected residue curve C_v over algebraically closed κ at each vertex and distinct marked points indexed by incident half-edges. Replace each vertex by C_v(κ) in the divisor support. A rational function is a PL graph function f_Γ with integral slopes and independent nonzero rational functions f_v on C_v. Its component divisor is div(f_v)+Σ_b slope_b(f_Γ)·p_b; its graph-interior divisor is divPL(f_Γ). The associated graph divisor puts total component degree at the vertex. Set K_C=Σ_v(K_{C_v}+Σ_bp_b), with genus b₁+Σg(C_v).
hypotheses: A loop has two distinct marked half-edge points on the same C_v; rational functions need not satisfy an unstated gluing equality.
proofSteps: Construct the free divisor group on graph interiors and residue-curve points. Refine at all breaks to prove total principal degree zero; moving vertex chips onto the corresponding component compares refined models.

nodes.title: Riemann–Roch and rank determination on complexes
nodes.statement: For a compact metrized complex C of genus g and any divisor D, r_C(D)−r_C(K_C−D)=deg D+1−g, using the combined graph/residue-curve principal-divisor convention.

nodes.title: Specialization inequality
nodes.statement: For a smooth proper connected curve X over algebraically closed complete nontrivial rank-one K and its semistable metrized complex C, specialization preserves principal divisors and r_X(D)≤r_C(sp D)≤r_Γ(τ_*D). The first map sends points above vertices to their residue point and points above graph interiors to their retraction. For f use the tuple (log|f||Γ, normalized reductions f_v), whose principal divisor is sp(div f).

proofSteps: The slope formula gives principal compatibility, including the marked-point terms. Choose the Appendix A rank-determining residue points and lift them to X(K); specialize every effective subtractand to obtain r_X≤r_C. For the second inequality lift a graph effective subtractand to arbitrary component points of matching degree and project the effective representatives.

nodes.title: Finite rank-determining sets
nodes.statement: Let C be a compact metrized complex with a loopless finite graph model G. For every vertex v choose any subset R_v⊂C_v(κ) of cardinality g(C_v)+1. The union R=∪_v R_v is rank determining: in the definition of r_C(D), it suffices to test effective subtractands supported on R. A graph loop must first be subdivided; points may be chosen away from the finitely many attaching points over algebraically closed κ.
hypotheses: κ algebraically closed; graph model loopless; the points in each R_v are distinct.
proofSteps: Use the v₀-reduced divisor characterization and continuity of the reduced-divisor map to find a test point in one R_v detecting failure of rank one. Subtract one test point and induct on the tested rank. Reduced-divisor existence and the continuity theorem are the exact open proof leaves.

nodes.title: Tropical multiplicity formula for curves
nodes.statement: K is algebraically closed and complete for a nontrivial rank-one nonarchimedean valuation; X is a smooth connected algebraic K-curve; X̂ is its smooth proper completion and D=X̂ minus X is the finite puncture set. After suitable subdivision, each tropical edge e′ has finitely many embedded segments e_i of H° mapping homeomorphically onto it. Other segments disjoint from these in its preimage are contracted. Its multiplicity is the sum of their positive integral expansion factors. Initial-degeneration components are counted with scheme multiplicities.
hypotheses: K is algebraically closed and complete for a nontrivial rank-one nonarchimedean valuation; X is a smooth connected algebraic K-curve; X̂ is its smooth proper completion and D=X̂ minus X is the finite puncture set.
proofSteps: For a value-group-rational tropical point, pass to its polyhedral analytic fiber and canonical reduction. The Shilov components account for the initial-degeneration generic lengths. For a curve, a finite annular projection identifies each relative component degree with its integral expansion factor. The finite-map reduction/multiplicity identity still requires a complete proof check.

nodes.statement: For finite-type X⊂T over any valued field, Trop(X)={w:in_w(X)≠∅}. It is the support of a finite v(K×)-rational polyhedral complex; if X is pure d-dimensional, it is pure d-dimensional. Local stars at w equal tropicalizations of in_w(X) over the trivially valued residue field.

nodes.title: Faithful tropicalization of a finite subgraph
nodes.statement: K is algebraically closed and complete for a nontrivial rank-one nonarchimedean valuation; X is a smooth connected algebraic K-curve; X̂ is its smooth proper completion and D=X̂ minus X is the finite puncture set. Metrics are the subgraph length metrics. H° is the non-leaf locus, excluding classical and type-4 points. This identifier now retains the existence part of Theorem 1.1.

proofSteps: Cover the finite embedded graph by finitely many closed skeletal segments. Use unit-slope functions to make the expansion gcd one, and add finitely many separating coordinates for pairs in distinct graph neighborhoods. The resulting toric refinement is locally isometric and injective on the compact graph, hence faithful.

nodes.title: Faithful tropicalization on a graph

nodes.title: Schottky groups and fundamental domains
nodes.statement: Use finitely generated Schottky subgroups Γ⊂PGL₂(K), equivalently in the marked presentation a free generating tuple γ₁,…,γ_g with pairwise disjoint paired closed discs D⁺(γ_i^{±1}) such that γ_i^{±1}(P¹ᵃⁿ\D⁺(γ_i^{∓1})) is the maximal open disc inside D⁺(γ_i^{±1}). Nonidentity elements are loxodromic. Their limit set Λ is the set of accumulation points of distinct group translates, and Ω=P¹ᵃⁿ\Λ. nodes.title: Schottky–Mumford uniformization
nodes.statement: For a rank-g Schottky group Γ, Ω→Γ\Ω is a free properly discontinuous analytic quotient, the quotient is a smooth proper split Mumford curve of genus g, and its skeleton is Γ\Hull(Λ) (with the limit endpoints removed before quotient). Conversely a split analytic Mumford curve is so uniformized. A split Mumford curve means locally a K-Swiss-cheese domain, equivalently a split semistable model whose normalized special components are P¹_κ and nodes are κ-rational. Potential total degeneration over a finite extension does not imply this split condition over K; descend with its Galois cocycle and graph action.
hypotheses: Complete nontrivially valued K. For the converse use the split Mumford hypothesis; genus zero gives P¹ and the trivial group, genus one the Tate quotient.
proofSteps: Reduced-word discs give a compact fundamental region, a free proper action and the hull skeleton; the genus formula gives genus g. For the converse, take the topological universal cover, exhaust its genus-zero tree by finite Swiss-cheese neighborhoods, cap boundary annuli and use Runge-compatible embeddings into P¹. Deck transformations extend to PGL₂(K), giving the Schottky group. The compatible Runge-embedding proof input is explicitly recorded.
acceptance: The quotient hull has b₁=g with all vertex genera zero.
A potentially split curve is kept with descent data, rather than declared a K-Schottky quotient without proof.

nodes.title: Analytic Jacobian periods
nodes.statement: For smooth proper X with split semistable model and Jacobian J, import its Raynaud analytic uniformization 0→M′→Eᵃⁿ→Jᵃⁿ→0, with 0→T→E→B→0 and B of good reduction. The valuation map trop:Eᵃⁿ→N_ℝ has ker on points the good-reduction domain, and trop(M′) is a full real lattice. For a split Mumford curve B=0, T has rank g, and Jᵃⁿ=Tᵃⁿ/M′. Under M′≅H₁(Σ,ℤ), the valuation of the multiplicative period pairing equals the edge-length pairing; hence Sk(J)≅Jac(Σ) as principally polarized real tori. The analytic Abel–Jacobi map retracts to the tropical Abel–Jacobi map.
hypotheses: Complete nonarchimedean K with split semistable model; choose X(K) basepoint when using the point Abel–Jacobi map. The Raynaud cross beyond the existing DVR formal comparison is a requested supplier statement.
proofSteps: Use the supplied uniformization and the specialization map on Pic⁰ induced by the slope formula. Compare the two Abel–Jacobi maps on divisors and integral cycles; the induced H₁ isomorphism identifies valuation periods with length integration. This identifies the principal polarizations, not merely the dimensions of the real tori.
acceptance: For a Tate curve the single multiplicative period is q and its valuation is L.
Good reduction gives toric rank zero, even when dim J>0.
The Cp-valued logarithmic periods need not form a discrete lattice; only their real valuation periods do.

nodes.title: Berkovich–Coleman path integration
nodes.statement: Fix a branch Log:ℂ_p×→ℂ_p extending the unit logarithm. For a smooth ℂ_p-analytic curve, and for the smooth analytic group covers used in the comparison, associate to a closed analytic 1-form and a continuous path with classical endpoints its Berkovich–Coleman integral. It is ℂ_p-linear in the form, invariant under endpoint-fixed homotopy, additive under path concatenation, functorial under analytic pullback, equals F(Q)−F(P) for exact dF, and satisfies ∫_P^Q dz/z=Log Q−Log P on G_m. Restriction to the good-reduction Coleman domains agrees with their Frobenius-normalized primitives.
hypotheses: Characteristic zero and ℂ_p; fixed branch; analytic closed forms and endpoint-fixed homotopy. No global endpoint-only primitive is asserted when the skeleton has cycles.
proofSteps: Glue local primitives/logarithmic annular primitives along a triangulation, retaining the path and continuation constants. On good-reduction pieces use the imported Coleman characterization. Independence and global existence require the Berkovich integration theorem beyond these local axioms; this is an explicit owned proof gap, not inferred from formal antiderivatives.

nodes.title: Annular integration and residue monodromy
nodes.statement: For an open annulus with coordinate t and ω=(Σa_ntⁿ)dt, import res(ω)=a₋₁ and its logarithmic primitive. The BC integral is a₋₁(Log t(Q)−Log t(P))+Σ_{n≠−1}a_n(t(Q)^(n+1)−t(P)^(n+1))/(n+1). Reversing annular orientation negates the residue; a branch change Log′−Log=c·v_p changes the value by c·res(ω)(v_p(t(Q))−v_p(t(P))). Residues of a regular differential around a semistable vertex sum to zero, defining a harmonic graph cochain. Cycle continuation of local primitives records BC periods and is distinct from the real monodromy length pairing.
hypotheses: Open annuli over ℂ_p; compatible Laurent convergence on every compact subannulus. For the vertex residue identity use regular differentials on a semistable proper curve.
proofSteps: Apply the imported annulus primitive and residue invariance. Laurent substitution proves the branch-change expression. On each normalized residue component the residue theorem cancels outgoing boundary residues; Čech continuation constants along graph cycles give periods. The semistable residue/continuation comparison is a stated proof leaf where absent from the local Coleman API.
acceptance: A residue-zero differential has an analytic annular primitive; dT/T does not.
A residue is a Cp scalar and an edge length is real: neither can replace the other in a period pairing.

nodes.title: BC–abelian tropical correction
nodes.statement: For an abelian variety A/ℂ_p with Raynaud cover E and torus cocharacter lattice N, let log_BC:E(ℂ_p)→Lie(A) be integration on its simply connected analytic cover and let log_Ab=log_A∘π be the imported analytic abelian logarithm. There is a unique ℚ-linear L:N_ℚ→Lie(A) with log_BC−log_Ab=L∘trop. For a path in A starting at 0 with lifted endpoint e, ∫_BC ω−∫_Ab ω=⟨L(trop e),ω⟩. For curve integrals compose with Abel–Jacobi. On an annulus the correction is a_ω(v_p(t(Q))−v_p(t(P))), linear in ω; on an open star of valence d, forms with zero correction have codimension at most d−1.
hypotheses: Use v_p(p)=1 for N_ℚ and Cp scalar arithmetic; convert natural-log graph lengths by log p. The abelian logarithm on all Cp-points is the analytic extension, not just a union of finite-extension point sets.
proofSteps: The two logarithms agree on the good-reduction domain A₀: the analytic group logarithm is uniquely characterized by its identity tangent map and agrees with local formal integration. Their difference therefore factors through E(Cp)/A₀(Cp)=N_ℚ. Restriction to the period lattice determines L since the real full lattice has ℚ-span N_ℚ. Tropical Abel–Jacobi balancing bounds the span of a d-star by d−1; an edge is one-dimensional, giving the annular coefficient.
acceptance: Good reduction has N=0, so BC and abelian integrals agree.
For E_q and dz/z, ∫_Ab=Log(z_Q/z_P)−(Log q/v_p(q))(v_p(z_Q)−v_p(z_P)), independent of changing lifts by q-powers.
On a valence-two annular star at most one linear condition makes the two integrals agree.
